examples.question_text: A cylindrical rod has a circular cross-section area of $15\text{ cm}^{2}$ and a length of $8\text{ cm}$. Find its volume.
examples.solution_text:
The length is the perpendicular distance between the circular ends.
$\begin{align*}V &= Ah\\&=15\times8\\&=120\text{ cm}^{3}\end{align*}$

The radius is $2\text{ cm}$ and the perpendicular height is the $13\text{ cm}$ length.
$\begin{align*}V &= \pi r^{2}h\\&=\pi\times2^{2}\times13\\&=52\pi\text{ cm}^{3}\\&\approx163.36\text{ cm}^{3}\end{align*}$

The radius is half the diameter.
$\begin{align*}r &= \frac{4}{2}=2\text{ m}\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}V &= \pi r^{2}h\\&=\pi\times2^{2}\times3\\&=12\pi\text{ m}^{3}\\&\approx37.7\text{ m}^{3}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A cylindrical tin has an internal radius of $3\text{ cm}$ and an internal height of $10\text{ cm}$. It contains $200\text{ cm}^{3}$ of paint. Find the empty space inside the tin, correct to two decimal places.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}V_{\text{tin}} &= \pi r^{2}h\\&=\pi\times3^{2}\times10\\&=90\pi\text{ cm}^{3}\end{align*}$
Subtract the paint volume from the tin’s internal volume.
$\begin{align*}V_{\text{empty}} &=90\pi-200\\&\approx82.74\text{ cm}^{3}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: Cylinder A has radius $3\text{ cm}$ and height $12\text{ cm}$. Cylinder B has diameter $8\text{ cm}$ and height $8\text{ cm}$. Find both volumes in exact form. State which is larger and find the difference, correct to two decimal places.
examples.solution_text:
Cylinder A:
$\begin{align*}V_A &=\pi\times3^{2}\times12\\&=108\pi\text{ cm}^{3}\end{align*}$
Cylinder B has radius $8\div2=4\text{ cm}$.
$\begin{align*}V_B &=\pi\times4^{2}\times8\\&=128\pi\text{ cm}^{3}\end{align*}$
Cylinder B has the greater volume.
$\begin{align*}\text{Difference} &=128\pi-108\pi\\&=20\pi\text{ cm}^{3}\\&\approx62.83\text{ cm}^{3}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A cylinder with radius $3\text{ cm}$ and height $6\text{ cm}$ fits exactly inside a cube with edge length $6\text{ cm}$. Express the cylinder’s volume as a percentage of the cube’s volume, correct to one decimal place.

A cylindrical container has internal radius $4\text{ cm}$ and internal height $10\text{ cm}$. It is full of water. The water is poured into an empty rectangular container with internal dimensions $10\text{ cm}$ by $8\text{ cm}$ by $7\text{ cm}$. Will all the water fit? Justify your answer using volumes correct to two decimal places.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}V_{\text{cylinder}} &=\pi\times4^{2}\times10\\&=160\pi\text{ cm}^{3}\\&\approx502.65\text{ cm}^{3}\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}V_{\text{box}} &=10\times8\times7\\&=560\text{ cm}^{3}\end{align*}$
All the water fits because $502.65\text{ cm}^{3}<560\text{ cm}^{3}$.

examples.derivation: Using the supplied cross-section area, V = Ah = 15 × 8 = 120 cm³. This follows Volume 3, Foundation Q1.
The diagram gives radius 2 cm and axial length 13 cm. V = π × 2² × 13 = 52π cm³ ≈ 163.36 cm³. Exact and rounded forms follow the supplied cylinder teaching and Foundation Q3.
The marked diameter is 4 m, so r = 2 m. V = π × 2² × 3 = 12π m³ ≈ 37.7 m³. Halving the diameter follows the second supplied worked example.
Internal volume = π × 3² × 10 = 90π cm³. Empty space = 90π − 200 = 82.743338… cm³ ≈ 82.74 cm³. Subtraction follows Volume 3, Development Q6.

VA = π × 3² × 12 = 108π cm³. Cylinder B has radius 4 cm, giving VB = π × 4² × 8 = 128π cm³. B is larger by 20π cm³ ≈ 62.83 cm³. Comparison follows Development Q7; subtraction is within the accepted assessed method.

Cylinder volume = π × 3² × 6 = 54π cm³; cube volume = 6³ = 216 cm³. Percentage = (54π ÷ 216) × 100 = 25π% ≈ 78.5%. The diameter and height both equal the cube edge, consistent with an exact fit. This follows Mastery Q12.
Water volume = π × 4² × 10 = 160π cm³ ≈ 502.65 cm³. Rectangular container volume = 10 × 8 × 7 = 560 cm³. All water fits because its volume is smaller. This follows Mastery Q14.
